blocks.title: Sample Spaces and Basic Probability
teacherCues: Ask: If you toss a single coin, what are the possible outcomes? Then toss two coins together – why do we list HT and TH separately?
Write the probability formula on the board. Ask: Can probability ever be negative or greater than 1?

discoveryHook.scenario: Every time you roll a die or flip a coin, chance decides the result. To measure your odds, you have to know all possible outcomes. That’s the sample space, and it’s the foundation of probability.

explanation: An [[kw:experiment]] is any happening with an uncertain result.
An [[kw:outcome]] is a single possible result; the [[kw:sample space]] $S$ is the set of all possible outcomes.
An [[kw:event]] $E$ is any subset of the sample space.
If all outcomes are equally likely, the [[kw:probability]] of event $E$ is $$P(E) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$$
Probability is always between $0$ and $1$: $0$ means impossible, $1$ means certain.

rows.1: $\{HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT\}$

formulaCard.title: Probability of an Event
notes: $n(E)$ = number of outcomes in the event.
$n(S)$ = number of outcomes in the sample space.
Applies when all outcomes are equally likely.

examples.title: A – Two Heads in Two Coins
examples.prompt: Toss two fair coins. What is the probability that both land heads up?
steps: Sample space $S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, so $n(S)=4$.

examples.title: B – Three Tails
examples.prompt: Toss three fair coins. Find the probability that all three land tails up.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: How many outcomes are in the sample space? Why is the event just one outcome?
steps: Sample space has $8$ outcomes (from the table).

examples.title: C – Drawing a Diamond
examples.prompt: Draw one card at random from a standard $52$‑card deck. What is the probability it is a diamond?
steps: There are $13$ diamonds in the deck.

confusionCorner.title: HT vs. TH
confusionCorner.body: When tossing two coins, we list $HT$ and $TH$ as separate outcomes even though they both show one head and one tail. This makes all outcomes [[imp:equally likely]], which is essential for the probability formula.

questions.prompt: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the ___.
hints: It contains every single result that could happen.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: That set is called the sample space.

questions.prompt: If an event is certain to happen, what is its probability?
hints: Certainty means it must occur every time.

questions.prompt: You roll a fair six‑sided die once. What is the probability of rolling a $5$? (Give as a reduced fraction, e.g., 1/6)
hints: There is one favorable outcome out of six.

blocks.title: Probability Using Counting Principles
teacherCues: Remind students of the Fundamental Counting Principle and combinations from Section 9.6.
Ask: If you toss two dice, how many total outcomes? Use $6 \times 6 = 36$.

discoveryHook.scenario: When the sample space is huge—like picking lottery numbers—you can’t list everything. This is where Section 9.6’s counting tools turn into probability tools.

explanation: To find $n(S)$ and $n(E)$ for large experiments, use the [[kw:Fundamental Counting Principle]], permutations, or combinations.
For equally likely outcomes, $$P(E) = \frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$$
Always check whether order matters; for example, a lottery drawing usually ignores order, so use [[kw:combinations]].

formulaCard.title: Probability with Counting
notes: Use the same counting method for $n(E)$ and $n(S)$.

examples.title: A – Sum of 7 on Two Dice
examples.prompt: You toss two fair six‑sided dice. What is the probability that the total is $7$?
steps: Favorable pairs (first die, second die): $(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)$ → $6$ ways.

examples.title: B – Sum of 5
examples.prompt: Using the same two dice, find the probability of rolling a sum of $5$.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: How many ordered pairs lead to a sum of 5, and why must we count both (1,4) and (4,1)?

examples.title: C – Lottery Ticket
examples.prompt: In a lottery, choose 5 different numbers from 1 to 43. If order doesn’t matter, what is the probability of winning with one ticket?

confusionCorner.title: Order Matters?
confusionCorner.body: In dice, the dice are distinct (one red, one blue), so $(1,6)$ and $(6,1)$ are different. In lotteries, order usually [[imp:doesn’t matter]], so we use combinations—not permutations—to count.

questions.prompt: When tossing two dice, how many total outcomes are there?
In a lottery where order does not matter, you should use ___ to count the number of possible tickets.
What is the probability of rolling a sum of $11$ with two dice? (Give a reduced fraction, e.g., 1/18.)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: There are 2 ways out of 36, so $P = 2/36 = 1/18$.

blocks.title: Mutually Exclusive Events and the Addition Rule
teacherCues: Draw two circles that do not overlap. Explain that events with no common outcomes are mutually exclusive.
Write the union formula and emphasize subtracting the intersection when events overlap.

discoveryHook.scenario: In a card game, you might care about ‘heart or face card’. These events overlap—some cards are both! To avoid double‑counting, we need a rule that handles the overlap.

explanation: Two events are [[kw:mutually exclusive]] if they cannot happen at the same time ($A \cap B = \emptyset$).
For any two events: $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, $P(A \cap B) = 0$, so the formula simplifies to $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$$

formulaCard.title: Union of Two Events
notes: If mutually exclusive, last term is $0$.

examples.title: A – Heart or Face Card
examples.prompt: Draw one card from a standard $52$‑card deck. Find the probability it is a heart or a face card.
steps: Overlap $A \cap B$ = heart face cards (J,Q,K of hearts): $P(A \cap B) = 3/52$.

examples.title: B – Sum of 6 or 9 on Dice
examples.prompt: Toss two dice. Find the probability the sum is $6$ or $9$.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why are these two events mutually exclusive? How do you find each probability?
steps: They can't happen at the same time → mutually exclusive.

examples.title: C – King or Spade
examples.prompt: From one draw of a $52$‑card deck, find the probability of drawing a king or a spade.

confusionCorner.title: Don’t Double‑Count
confusionCorner.body: If you just add $P(A) + P(B)$, you double‑count the outcomes that are in both events. Always [[imp:subtract the intersection]] unless you know they have no overlap.

questions.prompt: Two events that cannot occur at the same time are called ___.
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, what is $P(A \cap B)$?
hints: Think about the meaning of 'no outcomes in common'.
It's the probability of the empty set.

questions.prompt: A card is drawn. What is the probability that it is a queen or a red card? (Give a reduced fraction, e.g., 7/13.)
hints: Queens: 4/52, red cards: 26/52, overlap: 2 red queens.

blocks.title: Independent Events and the Complement Rule
teacherCues: Ask: If you flip a coin and roll a die, does the coin affect the die? No → independent events.
Write $P(\text{not }E) = 1 - P(E)$ and ask: How could we find the probability of not drawing an ace?

discoveryHook.scenario: A space probe has a main computer and a backup. They work independently, so the chance both fail is tiny. Calculating reliability uses the product rule for independent events and the complement for survival.

explanation: Two events are [[kw:independent]] if the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other.
For independent events $A$ and $B$: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)$$
The [[kw:complement]] of an event $E$, denoted $E'$ or $\overline{E}$, is the set of outcomes not in $E$.

formulaCard.title: Independent Events & Complement
notes: Check independence carefully: drawing without replacement makes events dependent.
Use the complement when 'not' is easier to count.

examples.title: A – Heads and a Six
examples.prompt: Flip a fair coin and roll a fair die. What is the probability of getting heads on the coin and a $6$ on the die?

examples.title: B – Both Aces with Replacement
examples.prompt: Draw two cards from a deck, replacing the first before drawing the second. Find the probability both are aces.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why does replacement make the draws independent? How would the calculation change without replacement?
steps: With replacement, the deck has $52$ cards each time → independent.

examples.title: C – Not an Ace
examples.prompt: Draw one card. Find the probability it is NOT an ace.

confusionCorner.title: Independent ≠ Mutually Exclusive
confusionCorner.body: Independent events can happen together (heads and a 6). Mutually exclusive events cannot. Don’t confuse them! If two events are mutually exclusive and have non‑zero probability, they are [[imp:dependent]] (knowing one happened tells you the other didn’t).

questions.prompt: When the outcome of one event does not influence the probability of another, the events are ___.
Two independent events each have probability $0.2$. What is the probability both occur?
If the probability of rain tomorrow is $0.3$, what is the probability it does NOT rain?

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid — Solving Probability Problems
teacherCues: Walk through the three‑step blueprint: Understand the experiment, Solve by counting favorable vs. total outcomes, Conclude with a clear probability statement.
Remind students to identify whether events are independent or mutually exclusive to choose the correct formula.

discoveryHook.scenario: When a problem mixes several events—like drawing marbles, flipping coins, or rolling dice—following a clear blueprint keeps you from getting lost. You’ll systematically break the problem into count‑and‑calculate steps.

explanation: Step 1 – [[kw:Understand]]: Define the sample space and the event. Decide if order matters, if events are independent, or if they are mutually exclusive.
Step 2 – [[kw:Solve]]: Use counting principles to find $n(S)$ and $n(E)$. For combined events, apply the addition rule (OR) or multiplication rule (AND for independent).
Step 3 – [[kw:Conclude]]: State the probability as a fraction, decimal, or percent in simplest form.

rows.0: Single event with equally likely outcomes

formulaCard.title: Probability Toolbox
formulaCard.formula: $$P(E) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)} \qquad P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$ $$P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B) \;\text{(indep)} \qquad P(E') = 1 - P(E)$$
notes: Choose the correct formula based on the wording.

examples.title: A – Both Red Marbles
examples.prompt: A bag has $4$ red, $5$ blue, and $6$ green marbles. Draw two without replacement. Find the probability both are red.
steps: Understand: Without replacement, draws are dependent. Total marbles = $15$.
Solve: $n(S) = {}_{15}C_2 = 105$; number of ways to pick $2$ red from $4$: ${}_{4}C_2 = 6$.

examples.title: B – Sum of 7 or 11 on Two Dice
examples.prompt: Find the probability of rolling a sum of $7$ or $11$ with two dice.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why are these two sums mutually exclusive? How would you compute each probability?
steps: Sum of 7: $6$ ways, $P = 6/36$; sum of 11: $2$ ways, $P = 2/36$.

examples.title: C – At Least One Six in Two Dice
examples.prompt: Toss two dice. Find the probability of getting at least one $6$.
steps: Easier: complement of no sixes. $P(\text{no six}) = (5/6)^2 = 25/36$.

confusionCorner.title: 'At Least One' Trick
confusionCorner.body: When you see 'at least one', the complement—'none'—is often much simpler to calculate. Then subtract from $1$.

questions.prompt: In a bag with $3$ red and $7$ blue marbles, you draw one marble. What is the probability it is NOT red?
The probability of an event $E$ not happening is found using the ___ rule.
You toss two fair coins. What is the probability of getting at least one head? (Give a reduced fraction, e.g., 3/4.)
hints: Complement: no heads means both tails ($1/4$).

challengeCorner.prompt: Two letters are chosen at random from the word 'APPLE', one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that both are P's?
hints: How many letters in the word? Which letters repeat?
Calculate the probability of drawing a P first, then a second P from the remaining letters.
challengeCorner.feedbackIfWrong: From 'APPLE': 2 P's out of 5. P(both P) = (2/5) × (1/4) = 2/20 = 1/10.
